8n35vs:199: In current agent research, there are three routes for memory/skill management: (1) manual curation (e.g., Anthropic Skills), which requires extensive human expert involvement and cannot scale; (2) heuristic methods, which rely on fixed rules and lack downstream performance feedback; (3) short-horizon RL adaptation, which only focuses on skill manipulation within immediate tasks and cannot handle complex management operations such as skill updates and deletions. SkillOS fills the gap of the third route—it uses task grouping and composite rewards to let the curator learn to make skill management decisions over long time spans.
960xkw:279: The paper uses GRPO (Grouped Reward Policy Optimization) to train the curator and finds that discarding the KL divergence term actually aids policy exploration. This finding has important engineering implications: the KL term is usually introduced to limit the magnitude of policy updates and prevent catastrophic forgetting, but in curation scenarios, excessive conservatism can hinder the curator from learning bold deletion and update operations. The curator needs to explore various combinations of insert/update/delete, and even attempt "destructive" operations to understand the boundaries of the skill repository. This freedom of exploration is crucial for learning effective long-term curation strategies. In practice, if a team requires more conservative curation behavior, they may consider adding the KL term in the later stages of training for fine-tuning, rather than constraining throughout.
